source.title: Do deep nets really need weight decay and dropout?

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper ablates weight decay and dropout on image-recognition tasks and argues they may be unnecessary when data augmentation is used. Its experiments do not test fitting random labels, but its results bear on V5's claim about regularizers and generalization.
record.gate_note: The study reports clean-label test accuracy under regularization and augmentation conditions. It does not report random-label fitting, shuffled or noise inputs, training time under label corruption, or learning order. Figure 1 results are described qualitatively in the text, with specific differences stated for WRN on CIFAR.
record.test_reason: The study directly tests V5's true-label generalization component by ablating weight decay and dropout and measuring held-out accuracy, following the original study's approach. It does not test random-label memorization.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: in the tested convolutional object-recognition settings, weight decay and dropout may be unnecessary when sufficient data augmentation is used, and augmentation alone can provide comparable generalization benefits.
record.recipe_differences: Ablation study of explicit regularization on All-CNN and WRN using ImageNet and CIFAR clean labels. Compared weight decay and dropout conditions with no augmentation, light augmentation, or heavier augmentation; did not use random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Data augmentation scheme and dataset/model combination change the reported outcome; authors also state that learning rate may be suboptimal after removing regularization.
record.problems: The study does not test random-label fitting, so it cannot establish whether weight decay or dropout prevent memorization. Results in Figure 1 are not numerically transcribed in the supplied text, and no uncertainty estimates are reported. The authors note that training hyperparameters may be suboptimal after removing regularization.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results found. Figure 1 shows condition-specific accuracy values, but the supplied text provides only qualitative descriptions and a few stated differences; no precise figure values were inferred.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, chance-level test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters under random labeling.
Relative training time and convergence as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and progressive test degradation across label-corruption fractions.

Whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation prevent fitting random labels; whether removing data augmentation itself preserves true-label generalization. Weight decay and dropout are removed jointly, so their individual necessity is not isolated.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy or random labels.

record.verdict_notes: Insignificant accuracy differences do not justify limits_scope for V5, which does not require identical accuracy after removing regularizers. States and verdicts concern only its tested true-label component. Exact augmentation-specific Figure 1 values are unavailable and already declared in rows_left_out; no statistical uncertainty estimates or formal significance tests are supplied.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label training error, chance test error, and whether architecture or training hyperparameters must change.
Training-time cost and convergence speed as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test error across levels of random label corruption.
The paper tests removing weight decay and dropout on true-label object-recognition tasks, but not whether these methods fail to stop fitting random labels.
Whether true-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.
